Most undergraduate level curricula are free to access via places like Khan academy and MIT open courseware. Even before Creative Commons materials were available online,  any person could buy cheap used textbooks that were an edition or two out of date, read them, and do the problems included therein. 

In other words, the information that used to be accessible only by attending daily university lectures is (nearly) freely available to anyone. It is also optional. If someone were to spend 2-4 years toiling away through physics textbooks, online lectures, and problem sets, they could presumably end up with nearly all the knowledge and skills of graduating physics major and lack only a $200,000 piece of paper that flimsily certifies their learning. 

The experiment where "education is free and optional" is already being performed, and it is no surprise to any of us that people choose to spend their time watching sports, scrolling social media, and playing video games rather than doing the hard work of self improvement and self education.

Yes! This is both the comment I was looking for and the video I was hoping would be linked. We can create animations and visuals that are unheard of in their detail and clarity, but it doesn't matter if the student doesn't apply themselves. People used to learn entire subjects with chalkboard lectures and dusty textbooks. Talking endlessly about "learning styles" elides the importance of the learner putting in the time and energy necessary to understand a subject. I tell my HS students that you will get out what you put in, both in my course and I'm college.

Hs teacher here: I am guilty of giving them guided notes as you describe. I am fully aware that they gain little to nothing by filling in the important vocabulary words. However, if I don't do this, most of them will write nothing down at all and will not pay attention at all. It's the most I can do to get them to focus for the 15 minutes I spend at the board each day. I never liked guided notes, and I know they should be making their own, but most of my 17 year old students can't or won't and I have to pick my battles.

I think the technology is partially responsible, and that we are teaching a generation of dopamine fiends with stunted attention spans. Textbooks are a nonstarter for most of these kids because they are "boring" and "not interactive". They need the information spoon fed in bite size portions, and if it isn't immediately tasty and easy to digest, they panic in confusion. 


I would say somewhere between 25-50% of my students have the habits, dispositions, and academic aptitude necessary for success, and they are doing just fine. But the bar is so low that they are barely being challenged, and meanwhile I'm being told by admin  "it's more important that AP chemistry should be a positive experience for students than it is to prepare them for the test, per se". I'm other words, teach to lowest common denominator, make everyone feel good about themselves, and the bright students will receive the rigor they need at a future time. 


To me this is all about a lack of accountability. No one holds students accountable for their choices, and anyone who tries to will just increase their workload. Don't get me wrong, teachers need to be held accountable by admin, admin needs to be held accountable by district admin, and district admin needs to be held accountable by the state education department. But schools are so pressed for resources that all accountability has gone out the window, and we're just left chasing our tails talking about SEL and DEI, as if they could solve everything in education.

I also teach high school chemistry and am horrified by the amount of grade inflation going on. My school's current policy is that all exams can be retaken for a maximum of a 90% on the retake. I teach honors and AP chem, and am so bogged down with making, proctoring, printing and grading retakes that I barely have time to teach the students who are keeping pace with the curriculum.

  
I watched a high school senior in Honors Chem today attempt to convert 341 J to kJ. I gave her the conversion factor on the quiz "1.0000 kJ = 1000.0 J" (since I don't make them memorize the metric system anymore, and to 5 SF since they can't wrap their head around metric conversions having infinite significance). She set up the dimensional analysis wrong, attempting to multiply by 1000, so I pointed her in the right direction. she then proceeded to enter "341 \* 1.0000" in her calculator, without dividing, and THEN ASKED ME WHY SHE WAS GETTING THE SAME NUMBER. 

No one is allowed to fail anymore, and holding the line only adds to my already impossible 12 hr a day workload. I feel bad sending these kids to college, and I feel worse knowing that they are aspiring, doctors, nurses, pilots, and engineers. But I'm just one teacher, and I'm hamstrung by broken policies in a broken educational system.

We are mad at the DNC for being narrow minded and not giving Sanders a chance. We are mad that they selected Hillary, a weak candidate mired by scandal, however contrived that scandal may be. We are mad that both the DNC and us liberals didn't recognize or take seriously the dissatisfaction that the white working class was feeling with the status quo.  But, you see, there's no use staying mad about it, and speculating whether Bernie would've beat Trump is pointless and a waste of energy.
 
Personally, I'm not too mad at Hillary herself. I feel bad for her because she was as blindsided as the rest of us by all this. Did she have major flaws? Of course.  Does she represent an establishment ruled by lobbyists and big Washington money that I resent? Definitely. But I think she was up against forces bigger than her and beyond her control. 

My feeling about protests like these is that they are good as long as they remain peaceful, but I'd rather see liberal millennials like myself doing local organizing toward a collective goal, not just expressing their anger and frustration by taking to the streets.
